originality.rationale: Searches of indexed mathematical claims, own accessible findings, and primary full-text hydrology sources did not establish a claim implying both the universal initially-empty three-pulse theorem and the four-pulse minimal counterexample. In particular the closest three-storm theorem is cyclic periodic, not transient; Gash-type canopy interception models and stochastic threshold-runoff results do not supply a fixed-input permutation theorem. This is a qualified historical-priority assessment: a general finite-dam or capped-recursion rearrangement theorem could dominate the result.
residual_risks: Historical priority is provisional: a general capped-recursion rearrangement or finite-dam theorem may subsume the three-pulse exchange despite different terminology.
The 1962 Gani–Pyke dam result was not available in full; conclusions are not asserted from its abstract.
The mathematical model is idealized and does not establish hydrologic field effect sizes or practical ability to reorder storms.

value.rationale: The minimum event count at which a seemingly plausible storm-magnitude-priority policy fails is a structural boundary relevant to interpreting idealized finite-capacity saturation-runoff and canopy bucket models. The all-parameter theorem and exact minimal counterexample demonstrate that small-event design conclusions cannot automatically be extrapolated to longer storm sequences; this is more than parameter tuning or a small numerical improvement. Hydrological transfer is conditional on model assumptions.
